topics.name: Boiling point
topics.kicker: The temperature where a liquid turns to gas · For water at sea level, 100 °C
topics.briefing: A liquid’s boiling point is the temperature where it turns into gas all the way through, sending bubbles of vapor rolling up from inside. For water at sea level that’s 100 °C (212 °F), but on top of Mount Everest the thin air lets water boil at only about 70 °C. Different substances have different boiling points, which is how oil refineries separate crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and other fuels.
topics.answerHtml: Boiling point (accept boiling temperature or normal boiling point; prompt on boiling; do not accept “vapor pressure”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Trouton’s rule says that for many liquids, the enthalpy of vaporization divided by this temperature in kelvins is roughly the same number. Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces, like the hydrogen bonds in water, have higher values of this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout, which is 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: Antifreeze in a car’s radiator lowers the coolant’s freezing point and also raises this temperature, so the coolant can get hotter without turning into a gas. Distillation separates the liquids in a mixture, such as the parts of crude oil, by differences in this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the pressure around it.

tossups.p: The rise in this temperature equals a constant called K-sub-b times the molality of the dissolved particles, and water’s value of that constant is about 0.512 degrees Celsius per molal. Dissolving salt or sugar raises this temperature, a colligative property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, 100 degrees Celsius for pure water at sea level.

tossups.p: IUPAC [“EYE-yoo-pak”] defines a “standard” version of this temperature at a pressure of 1 bar, which puts water’s at about 99.6 degrees Celsius. On the Kelvin scale, water’s ordinary value of this temperature is 373.15.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, 212 degrees Fahrenheit for water at sea level, at which a liquid turns into a gas.

tossups.p: When Anders Celsius created his temperature scale in 1742, he put 0 degrees at this temperature for water and 100 degrees at water’s freezing point. On the summit of Mount Everest, water reaches this temperature at only about 70 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is lower on mountaintops because the air pressure is lower.

tossups.p: The old Réaumur [“RAY-oh-myoor”] temperature scale put water’s value of this temperature at 80 degrees. On a heating curve, this temperature shows up as a flat stretch, because the added heat turns liquid into gas instead of making it hotter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

tossups.p: In the Leidenfrost [“LYE-den-frost”] effect, drops of water skitter across a pan far hotter than this temperature, riding on a cushion of gas. Chemists add porous chips to flasks so that liquids heated past this temperature form bubbles smoothly instead of suddenly erupting, a problem called bumping.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: A hypsometer [“hip-SOM-uh-ter”] estimates how high up a mountain you are by measuring water’s value of this temperature, which drops as you climb. Evaporation happens at a liquid’s surface at any temperature, but at this temperature bubbles of gas form all through the liquid.
tossups.r: For water at sea level, it is 212 degrees Fahrenheit. For 10 points, name this temperature, which is raised inside a pressure cooker.

tossups.p: Deep inside a geyser, the pressure of the water above raises this temperature, so the water there gets far hotter than it could at the surface before it suddenly flashes into steam. Liquid nitrogen’s value of this temperature is about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout.

tossups.p: Branched molecules have lower values of this temperature than their straight-chain isomers, so neopentane’s is far below pentane’s. In the alkanes, this temperature climbs as the carbon chains get longer, so methane through butane are gases at room temperature but pentane is a liquid.
tossups.r: Distillation separates liquids by differences in this temperature. For 10 points, name this temperature, 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: The Clausius–Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] equation can predict how this temperature changes when the outside pressure changes. Helium has the lowest value of this temperature of any element, about 4 kelvins, and liquid nitrogen’s is about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the pressure of the surrounding air.

tossups.p: Carbon dioxide has no value of this temperature at ordinary air pressure, because dry ice turns straight into gas without melting. On a heating curve, this temperature appears as a flat stretch while liquid turns into gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which water reaches at 212 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level.

tossups.p: An azeotrope [“ay-ZEE-uh-trohp”] is a mixture whose gas has the same makeup as its liquid at this temperature, so ordinary distillation cannot separate it. Oil refineries split crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and other fuels using differences in this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is 100 degrees Celsius for pure water at sea level.

tossups.p: A spoonful of salt in a pot of pasta water raises this temperature by only a tiny fraction of a degree. Adding a nonvolatile solute always raises this temperature, an effect called a colligative property because it depends only on the number of dissolved particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is lower on mountaintops and higher inside a pressure cooker.

tossups.p: Hydrogen sulfide molecules are heavier than water molecules, yet hydrogen sulfide is a gas at room temperature, because water’s hydrogen bonds give it a much higher value of this temperature. Among similar compounds, bigger molecules usually have higher values of this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout, 100 degrees Celsius for water.

trap.title: Temperature, not pressure
trap.body: This temperature and vapor pressure are two halves of one idea: a liquid reaches this temperature when its vapor pressure climbs to match the outside pressure. So clues about Raoult’s law or pressure cookers tempt players to say “vapor pressure,” and others mix this temperature up with the melting point or freezing point. Saying just “boiling” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “this temperature”: 100 °C for water, lower on mountains, raised by dissolved salt, and used to separate liquids by distillation. “This quantity” or “this pressure” that rises as a liquid warms means vapor pressure; solid turning to liquid means the melting point.
trap.line: Real answer line: Boiling point (accept boiling temperature; prompt on boiling; do not accept “vapor pressure”)

topics.name: Marie Curie
topics.kicker: Pioneer of radioactivity · First person to win two Nobel Prizes
topics.briefing: Marie Curie grew up in Warsaw, Poland, where women were not allowed to attend university, so she moved to Paris and became one of the greatest scientists in history. With her husband, Pierre, she discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, and she coined the word “radioactivity.” She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win two, in physics in 1903 and in chemistry in 1911.
topics.answerHtml: Marie Curie (accept Maria Skłodowska, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, or Madame Curie; prompt on Curie; do not accept “Pierre Curie” or “Irène Joliot-Curie”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young woman, this scientist attended a secret “Flying University,” because the official university in her city did not admit women. She later named one of the elements she discovered after her homeland, which was then divided among three empires.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist who discovered radium and won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.

tossups.p: This scientist measured the tiny electric currents that uranium’s rays produce in air, using an electrometer built by her husband and his brother Jacques, who had discovered the piezoelectric effect. She was following up on Henri Becquerel’s 1896 discovery that uranium gives off mysterious rays.
tossups.r: She went on to discover polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: In 1898, this scientist found that thorium also gives off radiation, independently of Gerhard Schmidt in Germany. She noticed that the uranium ore pitchblende was far more radioactive than its uranium alone could explain.
tossups.r: That led her to discover polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: This scientist’s 1903 doctoral thesis was titled _Research on Radioactive Substances_. She did much of the work behind it with her husband in a drafty, leaky shed, where they processed tons of ore.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own.

tossups.p: In 1921, U.S. President Warren Harding presented this scientist with one gram of radium, bought with money raised by American women. She founded the Radium Institute in Paris, and a sister institute later opened in her hometown.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: In 1995, this scientist’s remains were moved to the Panthéon [“pahn-tay-OHN”] in Paris, making her the first woman buried there for her own achievements. After her husband died in a street accident in 1906, she became the first woman to be a professor at the University of Paris.
tossups.r: She won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry. For 10 points, name this discoverer of polonium and radium.

tossups.p: This scientist was nearly left out of the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics until her husband insisted that her work be honored too. The couple processed tons of ore in a drafty, leaky shed to collect tiny amounts of a new, faintly glowing element.
tossups.r: That element was radium. For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: This scientist died in 1934 of aplastic anemia, a blood disease probably caused by years of handling radioactive materials. Her daughter Irène and Irène’s husband, Frédéric Joliot [“zhoh-LYOH”], shared the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who discovered radium and polonium with her own husband, Pierre.

tossups.p: In 1910, this scientist and André-Louis Debierne isolated radium as a pure metal. She named radium after the Latin word for “ray,” and its compounds glow faintly in the dark.
tossups.r: Element 96, curium, is named for her and her husband. For 10 points, name this scientist who won two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: This scientist realized that radiation must come from inside atoms, because a sample’s radiation depended only on how much uranium it held, not on its chemical form. She built on Henri Becquerel’s discovery of the rays given off by uranium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: In 1911, the French Academy of Sciences narrowly voted not to admit this scientist as a member. During World War I, she set up mobile X-ray units in cars to help army doctors treat wounded soldiers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-time Nobel Prize winner who discovered polonium and radium.

tossups.p: This scientist’s first research project in Paris studied the magnetic properties of different steels, and while looking for lab space for it, she met the French physicist she married in 1895.
tossups.r: With him, she later discovered polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: This scientist and her husband chose not to patent their method for purifying radium, so that other scientists could use it freely. She founded the Radium Institute in Paris, which became a leading center for research on radiation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: In 1902, after years of processing pitchblende, this scientist finally isolated about a tenth of a gram of radium chloride. That ore was far more radioactive than its uranium could explain, which convinced her that it held new elements.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who discovered polonium and radium and won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

tossups.p: This scientist worked for years as a governess to help pay for her older sister Bronisława’s medical studies in Paris, before following her there to study physics. She named one of the elements she discovered after her homeland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

trap.title: Which Curie?
trap.body: Three Curies won Nobel Prizes: this scientist, her husband Pierre (who shared the 1903 Physics prize), and their daughter Irène Joliot-Curie (the 1935 Chemistry prize, with her husband Frédéric Joliot). Saying just “Curie” earns only a prompt, and naming the wrong family member loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Growing up in Warsaw, the Flying University, a second Nobel Prize in 1911, and naming polonium all mean this scientist. Pierre clues: piezoelectricity with his brother Jacques and the Curie temperature of magnets. Irène clues: making new radioactive elements and the 1935 prize. Always include her first name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Marie Curie (accept Maria Skłodowska; prompt on Curie; do not accept “Pierre Curie” or “Irène Joliot-Curie”)
